prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and the Z2 topological insulator, and the first experimental realization of the quantum spin Hall state in HgTe quantum wells

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged from round 1: B013 with Kane, Mele and Molenkamp, as a single prize part. The chair asks what standard of maturity we should apply between B025 and B013, and my answer is that the discovery credited must have a stable interpretation as well as a stable phenomenology. For topological insulators it does. Kane and Mele introduced the Z2 invariant and the quantum spin Hall state, Molenkamp's group observed helical edge transport in HgTe wells, and nearly two decades of transport, photoemission and scanning-probe work in many materials have confirmed the picture, including the bulk-boundary correspondence that gives the idea its force. It is a complete chain from a concept to a discovery about nature, and it changed how condensed matter classifies phases. The round-1 exchange also settled for me that the B033 framing should stay set aside: Eriksson, Johansson, Lindroth and Olsson all showed that bundling the quantum anomalous Hall effect in with the quantum spin Hall effect makes a compound citation with a separate experimental programme (Xue, building on Haldane's model) and cuts the chain at inconvenient places, and dropping Mele to make room for Xue inverts the priority of the originating idea. The citation should be confined to the two-dimensional quantum spin Hall effect and the Z2 concept. That also answers the chair's question about Lindroth's Kane, Molenkamp and Hasan set: Hasan's three-dimensional identification is a distinct discovery, and I would not give it a seat by removing half of the Kane-Mele paper.
statement.case_against: The credit remains compound, and I want that on the record rather than hidden by the citation wording. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang predicted the HgTe quantum spin Hall state that motivated the Molenkamp experiment and are not an available name; Hasan's three-dimensional photoemission work is a separate achievement that a three-name set cannot also honour; and the HgTe edge quantization is imperfect in practice. The 2016 prize on topological phases and phase transitions may make some members reluctant to return to topology so soon. I think Olsson is right that the overlap is limited, since that prize concerned bulk topological invariants in the quantum Hall setting and topological phase transitions, whereas the symmetry-protected time-reversal class is different, but the committee should expect the objection. Practical impact so far is mainly conceptual. Against B025, the open pairing mechanism, twist-angle disorder and the Andrei priority question still weigh with me on timing, though I accept that they bear on maturity and not on the existence of the phenomena.

responses.point: Argues that twisted bilayer graphene revealed a previously unknown regime of correlated electrons, that the phenomenology is secure and widely reproduced even with the pairing mechanism open, and that earlier prizes honoured established effects without a settled microscopic explanation.
responses.response: This is the strongest argument against my position and I have moved on part of it. I accept that the credited discovery is the existence of correlated insulators and gate-tunable superconductivity at the magic angle, and that an open pairing mechanism does not by itself disqualify a prize, since the committee has honoured effects before their explanation was complete. I have therefore kept B025 as my first alternative and I would not call it premature in the sense of being wrong. Where I still differ is on what the committee can say with confidence. For topological insulators the phenomenon and the interpretation are both settled after nearly twice the time, whereas for B025 the discovery is secure but the field is still reorganising itself around the mechanism, strain and disorder, and a seat in the three-name set must be taken from Andrei or Bistritzer. I also note that your own statement offers B013 as the safer prize if the committee finds the field too fluid, and that is the judgement I am making.

responses.point: Prefers B013 with Kane, Mele and Molenkamp, argues the 2016 prize overlap is limited, and would keep the citation to the quantum spin Hall state and topological insulators and leave the quantum anomalous Hall effect to a later, separate consideration.
responses.response: I agree with your handling of the quantum anomalous Hall effect and I now accept your argument against swapping Mele for Xue: the Z2 paper is the conceptual origin, and Xue's realization rests on Haldane's model and a separate magnetic-doping programme, so it belongs to a later and separate consideration. My B033 ballot was a mistake in this respect, and I withdraw it from my alternatives. I also find your account of the 2016 overlap persuasive, the time-reversal-symmetric Z2 class being a different object from the bulk quantum Hall invariant, though I would keep it as a stated uncertainty. Where I would press you is on the wording of the citation. 'Topological insulators' in the citation risks reading as a claim on the three-dimensional materials, which Hasan's work established, so I prefer to name the quantum spin Hall effect and the Z2 invariant explicitly and keep the HgTe experiment as its realization.

responses.point: Prefers B006 with Katori and Ye as a mature, two-name, discovery-plus-instrument case, says it rests on the 2005 and 2012 prizes without duplicating them, and questions the compound credit in the topological insulator case, asking the committee to settle explicitly how three slots are allocated among Kane, Mele, Molenkamp and Hasan.
responses.response: You asked for an explicit decision on the third slot and I will give mine: Kane, Mele and Molenkamp, with Hasan treated as a distinct three-dimensional discovery that this prize does not cover, and with the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang prediction acknowledged as unavailable. I do not think the larger opening support for the topic should stand in for that decision, and I agree that attribution cleanliness matters. On B006 I accept that Katori and Ye is the cleanest attribution on the shortlist, that its maturity is not in doubt and that the redefinition of the second should not decide the matter. My remaining difference is one of weighting, not of quality: I read the lattice clock as a very large gain in an already honoured metrological line, and I place a new classification of electronic matter somewhat higher. Since you and Kroll both ask for consistent treatment of nearby prizes, I note that the same restraint I apply to circuit QED I should also apply to B006, which is why I would not call the 2005 and 2012 overlap fatal, only a relevant consideration. I now list B006 among my alternatives.

responses.point: Prefers B025 as a clean prediction-then-discovery pair with timing that looks ripe, calls B013 a close second, and says the compound attribution in B013 makes the three-name cut more arbitrary than in B025.
responses.response: I accept that B025 maps one prediction and one experiment onto three names more directly than B013 does, and that this is a real advantage in attribution. I would dispute that the B013 cut is more arbitrary, though. Kane and Mele's joint paper and Molenkamp's experiment form the credited chain, and the omissions are a theory proposal (Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang) that identified the material, and a separate three-dimensional discovery. That is a contestable edge but not a break in the chain. In B025 the cut goes through the Bistritzer-MacDonald pair or through Andrei, and you yourself call that seat the most contestable. We agree that either citation must stay on the observed phenomena. I would add that your support for Andrei if the committee preferred it shows the B025 set is less stable than the B013 trio, which five of the eight openings named.

responses.point: Moved B025 to the head of the configuration after reading all eight ballots, argues that the open mechanism must be separated from the existence of the phases, and asks that the topological-insulator line be considered as one coherent topic with the Hasan and Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang credit debated openly.
responses.response: I agree that B013 should be treated as one coherent topic and that the credit question is best debated openly, which is what I have done above: I keep the citation to the two-dimensional quantum spin Hall effect and exclude Hasan on principle, not by omission. I also agree with your distinction between the open mechanism and the established phases, and it is the reason I no longer say B025 is premature. I take your point that breadth of support across members from different subfields is informative, though I would still want that support weighed against the Andrei and Bistritzer problem, which you say you cannot settle from the supplied ballots. If the final vote shows the committee prefers B025, I could support the MacDonald, Bistritzer, Jarillo-Herrero trio with a citation anchored on flat bands and the first correlated and superconducting states, as you propose, and not on moire physics at large.

uncertainties: Whether the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang HgTe prediction and Hasan's three-dimensional work can be set aside fairly, given that they are outside the three credited names and no configuration can include them.
Whether the 2016 prize on topological phases weighs against a further topology prize now; I judge the overlap limited but cannot be certain how colleagues will read it.
Whether the open pairing mechanism, twist-angle disorder and Andrei's early flat-band evidence make B025 premature, or only a matter of timing that a few years will resolve.

Whether the committee should state an explicit rule on recent prizes in nearby fields (2005, 2012, 2016, 2025) and apply it equally across B013, B006, B025 and B009; I would support such a rule but have not settled how heavily it should count.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile. My professional connections (David Gross, Hector Rubinstein, Thomas Van Riet, the Uppsala theory group) are in string theory and gravity and none of the credited candidates is among them. I remain a formal theorist and may tend to favor a concept with a clean theoretical core, which could bias me toward a prediction-led case such as B013 and I flag that for colleagues to weigh.
